newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CRICKET-WARNE RETURNS TO TEST ARENA WITHOUT SUCCESS.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-WARNE RETURNS TO TEST ARENA WITHOUT SUCCESS.

text.p: Master wrist spinner Shane Warne returned to test cricket on Saturday after a lengthy absence because of injury but his appearance answered few questions about his long-term future as a wicket-taker.
Warne, Australia's main strike bowler, delivered relatively gentle overs of leg-spin without reward as Australia took control of the first test against West Indies at the Gabba.

The Victoria captain underwent surgery to repair ligament damage on the ring finger of his bowling hand in May, raising some concerns as to whether he will ever regain his ability to spin the ball prodigiously.
Introduced into the attack late in the day with the opposition under intense pressure -- circumstances which he has relished in the past -- Warne produced an unthreatening spell.
"He appeared to be playing himself back in," said former English county player and cricket writer Peter Roebuck, a keen observer of all Warne's home test matches in recent years.
"Shane was definitely bowling slower than he did last year. He was getting a little bounce and spin but there was less energy on the ball.

"I don't think we will know for another month or so whether he can recapture his form and be the same force again in test cricket," Roebuck said, referring to Warne's impressive record of 207 wickets in 44 previous test appearances.
In his five overs on Saturday, Warne failed to beat the bat and conceded 12 runs, including one sublime off-drive for four by West Indian number three Brian Lara.
Warne has bowled only sparingly by his own standards for Victoria this season and, according to local media, he still suffers swelling in the joint after bowling.

Australia wicketkeeper Ian Healy, the man best able to assess Warne's form, refused to judge his performance on Saturday against his past outings at the Gabba, where he took a career-best eight for 71 against England two years ago.
"He played pretty well and he is already looking to exploit the bowlers' footmarks," Healy said of his team mate.
"He is probing away and I think the pitch will help him as the match progresses."
But Healy declined to give his opinion when asked if Warne was imparting as much spin on the ball as in the past.
"I don't know the amount of effort he's putting in with his finger. You will have to ask Shane, I just can't answer that," Healy said.
At close of play on the second day, West Indies were 61 for two in reply to Australia's 479 all out.
